must_remember: Ferrimagnetic materials contain magnetic ions distributed over at least two different crystallographic sublattices (A and B) with antiparallel coupling.
Net spontaneous magnetization arises because the magnetic moments on the two sublattices are unequal in magnitude or number per unit volume ($M = |M_B - M_A|$).
Common ferrimagnetic oxides are spinels with the general chemical formula $\text{MO}\cdot\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$, where $\text{M}$ is a divalent metal ion.
The critical temperature above which a ferrimagnet becomes paramagnetic is called the Néel temperature ($T_N$).
In the paramagnetic region ($T > T_N$), the inverse magnetic susceptibility $1/\chi$ exhibits a hyperbolic asymptote due to negative inter-sublattice molecular field coefficients.
At the compensation temperature ($T_{comp}$), the sublattice magnetizations balance out ($M_A = M_B$), causing the net spontaneous magnetization to momentarily drop to zero.
Unlike pure metals, most practical ferrimagnets (ferrites) are ceramic insulators or semiconductors possessing very high electrical resistivity.

glossary.meaning: Crystallographic sites in ferrimagnetic lattices occupied by metal ions, specifically tetrahedral (A) and octahedral (B) sites.
The critical transition temperature above which thermal agitation overcomes magnetic ordering, rendering a ferrimagnet paramagnetic.
An indirect exchange coupling between magnetic ions mediated through intermediate non-magnetic oxygen anions.
A specific temperature below $T_N$ where the net magnetization vanishes because sublattice magnetizations $M_A$ and $M_B$ are equal.
The non-linear behavior of inverse magnetic susceptibility $1/\chi$ as a function of temperature above $T_N$ in ferrimagnets.
A crystal structure class for ferrites represented by $\text{MO}\cdot\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ containing interstitial tetrahedral and octahedral sites.
